## Overview

The Natukhai are one of the twelve major Circassian tribes and represent one of the twelve stars on the green-and-gold Circassian flag. Their historical territory extended along the Black Sea coast from Anapa in the north to Tsemes Bay, now Novorossiysk, in the south, and from the north side of the mountains to the lower Kuban River. Today, Natukhaj families live in the diaspora and have been assimilated into other Adyghe tribes, more precisely the Shapsug. In Russia, a few Natukhaj people are found in the Republic of Adyghea, mainly in the Takhtamukaysky District and the Teuchezhsky District.

## Festivals & rituals

The Natukhai were one of the last tribes to convert to Islam. They adhered steadily to Christianity, and religious differences often caused quarrels with the neighbouring Shapsug. By the beginning of the 19th century, a Turkish pasha persuaded them to convert to Islam, whether by promises or threats.

In late 1860, a Circassian Parliament, *Хасэ*, romanized as Hasè, was assembled to unite the Shapsug, Ubykh, and Natukhai. Sochi, given in the sources as Lowland Adyghe *Шъачэ* and Ubykh Adyghe *Шуа-чӀа*, was considered the last capital of the Circassian resistance.

## Foodways

They state that the Natukhai were active in trading with the Ottoman Empire and Crimean Khanate and established trade connections with Turkey.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Natukhai include the tribe of Guaye, which, according to the source, is one of the most ancient Circassian tribes according to legend. The sources also state that the Natukhai include the disappearing remnants of the Zhaney tribe. No Natukhai folktales, epic poems, proverbs, riddles, storytelling contexts, literary works, or preservation efforts are described.

## Language & religion

The Natukhai speak the Natukhai sub-dialect, *НатIхъуаджэбзэ*, an Adyghe dialect very similar to the Shapsug sub-dialect. The Natukhai sub-dialect shares many features with other Shapsug varieties. It has the consonants *гь* [ɡʲ], *кь* [kʲ], *кӏь* [kʲʼ], and *чъу* [t͡ɕʷ], corresponding in other Adyghe sub-dialects to *дж* [d͡ʒ], *ч* [t͡ʃ], *кӏ* [t͡ʃʼ], and *цу* [t͡sʷ]. The sources name Abzakh, Bzhedug, and Temirgoy as examples of other Adyghe sub-dialects.

The Natukhai maintained Christianity for a long period and converted to Islam only by the beginning of the 19th century.
